title: Association between traffic-related black carbon exposure and lung function among urban women.
ehr_evidence: Women were voluntary participants in the Maternal–Infant Smoking Study of East Boston, a prospective cohort originally designed to study the effects of pre- and postnatal tobacco smoke exposure on childhood lung growth and development and respiratory health.
summary: In a prospective community-based cohort of 272 urban women aged 18–42 years in East Boston, long-term estimated traffic-related black carbon exposure was associated with modestly decreased percent predicted lung function (FEV1, FVC, FEF25–75%).
key_findings: In adjusted analysis, black carbon per IQR increase (0.22 µg/m3) was associated with a 1.1% decrease in FEV1 (95% CI, –2.5 to 0.3%), a 0.6% decrease in FVC (95% CI, –1.9 to 0.6%), and a 3.0% decrease in FEF25–75% (95% CI, –5.8 to –0.2%).

There was a significant interaction with smoking status: former smokers had significant reductions in FEV1 (–4.4%), FVC (–3.1%), and FEF25–75% (–8.9%, all p < 0.05), whereas current smokers had no significant effects.
No significant exposure-response relationship was found across BC tertiles (FEV1 p = 0.2, FVC p = 0.3, FEF25–75% p = 0.10).
population: 272 urban women aged 18–42 years (mean 26.9) in East Boston, Massachusetts, recruited during pregnancy from a community health center
limitations: Significant reduction in sample size from the original cohort over time (loss to follow-up).
Possible unmeasured or residual confounding, particularly by socioeconomic status.
Use of predicted (modeled) exposure rather than observed measurements, introducing potential Berkson-type measurement error and invalid standard errors.
No information on other spatially variable pollutants (e.g., nitrogen dioxide, ozone) for comparison.
Limited variability in individual-level SES due to recruitment from a single neighborhood health center.
